# Introduction

Cluster randomized trials (CRTs) randomize intact groups, such as clinics, schools, or geographic areas, rather than individuals, and are the standard design when an intervention is delivered at the group level or when individual randomization would create unacceptable contamination between arms [@donner_design_2000; @hayes_cluster_2017]. A central assumption underlying standard CRT analysis is the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA): a control cluster's outcome must not depend on which other clusters were assigned to treatment [@hudgens_toward_2008]. This assumption, borrowed from individually randomized trial theory, is routinely violated once clusters are spatially arranged. Tobler's first law of geography, "everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things" [@tobler_computer_1970], implies that an intervention delivered in one location can plausibly influence outcomes in geographically adjacent locations through shared populations, service networks, information diffusion, or environmental pathways. Documented examples of this kind of spatial spillover span public health and development economics: distributing insecticide-treated bed nets in one Ghanaian village reduced child mortality in neighboring villages that did not themselves receive nets [@binka_impact_1998], and deworming interventions delivered in treated Kenyan schools reduced infection prevalence in nearby untreated schools through reduced transmission [@miguel_worms_2004]. When spillover of this kind is present but unmodeled, standard CRT estimators are biased, and both the direction and the magnitude of that bias depend on the spatial arrangement of treated and control clusters relative to one another, not merely on the number of clusters allocated to each arm.

## The design-stage gap in the spatial interference literature

The methodological literature addressing spatial interference in CRTs has concentrated overwhelmingly on analysis-stage correction. Spatial autocorrelation statistics such as Moran's $I$ [@moran_interpretation_1948; @moran_notes_1950] and Geary's $C$ [@geary_contiguity_1954] provide tools for detecting residual spatial dependence once outcomes have been observed, and spatial regression models, including spatial lag and spatial Durbin specifications [@lesage_introduction_2009], estimated by maximum likelihood [@ord_estimation_1975] and implemented in modern software [@bivand_r_2022], allow an analyst to separate a direct treatment effect from a spillover effect after the fact. In their systematic review of spatial analysis methods for cluster randomized trials, Jarvis and colleagues placed trials that used spatial separation or buffers outside the primary review of statistical methods [@jarvis_spatial_2017]. The literature therefore offers much more guidance on analyzing spatial effects than on how the choice of treatment assignment itself, made before any data are collected, might limit the problem at its source.

Design-stage tools do exist, but they were largely developed for a different purpose. Restricted randomization addresses the baseline imbalance that a limited number of clusters can produce [@raab_balance_2001]. Covariate-constrained randomization generates candidate assignments, retains those meeting a prespecified covariate-balance criterion, and randomizes among them [@moulton_covariatebased_2004]; Crisp and colleagues extended it to the selection of clusters from a larger eligible set and noted that their procedure also increases spatial dispersion among the selected clusters [@crisp_covariate-constrained_2023]. None of these methods was developed with spatial spillover specifically in mind; balancing a covariate across arms does not by itself determine whether treated and control clusters are spatially interspersed in a way that induces contamination. A more recent body of work addresses the problem studied in this chapter more directly. Randomized saturation designs deliberately vary the intensity of treatment across experimental units, which allows direct and spillover effects to be jointly identified rather than merely controlled for [@baird_optimal_2018]. In the malaria control literature, a conventional "fried-egg" design omits each cluster's outer area from analysis to limit contamination; McCann and colleagues proposed instead selecting whole clusters for inclusion or exclusion while preserving randomization [@mccann_spatial_2018]. Most recently, a cluster of theoretical papers published or posted between 2022 and 2025 has derived rate-optimal cluster-randomized designs under spatial interference [@leung_rateoptimal_2022], independent-set designs under network interference [@cai_independentset_2023], designs that explicitly account for cross-cluster interference [@leung_clusterrandomized_2025], and designs for spatio-temporally heterogeneous treatment effects [@watson_design_2025]. Taken together, this recent work moves toward design-stage solutions to spatial interference, but it has not yet produced a systematic, simulation-based comparison of concrete design strategies under realistic, heterogeneous spatial conditions of the kind a trial team would actually face when planning a study.

## Extending a small-grid proof of concept

This chapter extends the proof-of-concept study of Chapter 2, which asked a narrower version of the same question: how does a priori treatment-assignment strategy affect estimation under spatial spillover and spatial dependence? That study compared simple random assignment against a single block-stratified design, on small, exhaustively enumerable grids of 8 to 12 spatial units arranged in $2\times4$, $3\times3$, and $3\times4$ configurations, and estimated the intervention effect with a spatial autoregressive (SAR) lag model containing a spillover indicator, with separate parameters for a baseline effect, the intervention effect, the spillover effect, and spatial dependence. Among its future considerations, Chapter 2 listed a broader range of grid dimensions and neighbor structures beyond rook contiguity. This chapter takes up both and adds two extensions that list did not include: a larger set of designs than a single alternative to simple random assignment, and heterogeneous, rather than spatially uniform, baseline outcome risk. We scale from 8--12 clusters to a 100-cluster grid, from two designs to six conceptually distinct treatment assignment strategies (with two additional statistically redundant variants reported in the supplementary material for completeness), and from a single, uniform baseline risk surface to three distinct mechanisms of heterogeneous baseline incidence, so that some of the designs under study can exploit prior knowledge of spatial risk patterns while others cannot.

## Aims

This chapter has three aims. First, to rank the six treatment assignment designs by estimation accuracy, measured by mean squared error (MSE), and by inferential validity, measured by 95\% confidence interval coverage, separately within each of the three incidence-heterogeneity mechanisms, since a design that performs well under one mechanism may not generalize to another. Second, to test whether that ranking is stable across the spatial and spillover parameters that a real trial team cannot control or know in advance, including the magnitude of the true treatment effect itself, the strength of residual spatial dependence in the outcome, and the magnitude of the spillover effect. Third, to translate the resulting ranking into concrete, actionable design guidance, illustrated using a real and currently developing application: a planned sudden unexpected death (SUD) prevention pilot to be delivered through North Carolina's community college network. The sections that follow describe the simulation methods, report results for each aim, present the SUD application, and discuss limitations and future work.

# Methods

## Spatial structure and outcome model

We simulated a $10\times10$ regular grid of 100 clusters under two definitions of adjacency. Under queen contiguity, two clusters are neighbors if they share an edge or a corner; under rook contiguity, they must share an edge. Queen contiguity is the primary analysis in this chapter. Rook contiguity is a sensitivity analysis and the case that continues Chapter 2, whose grids used rook neighbors. For each definition, the binary adjacency matrix was row-standardized to form the spatial weights matrix $W$, so that $WZ$ gives, for each cluster, the proportion of its neighbors that are treated, and $WY$ gives the average outcome among its neighbors. Row-standardization expresses each cluster's spillover exposure as an average over its own neighborhood rather than a raw sum, which would otherwise depend on how many neighbors the cluster has. Within a scenario, the same neighbor type defines $W$ in the outcome model, in the Isolation Buffer design, and in the fitted model.

Cluster-level outcomes $Y$ were generated from a spatial lag model with a spillover term,
$$
Y = (I - \rho W)^{-1}\left[\tau Z + S(Z) + \beta X + \epsilon\right], \qquad \epsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2 I), \tag{1}
$$
where $Z \in \{0,1\}^{100}$ is the treatment assignment produced by the design under evaluation, $\tau$ is the direct treatment effect of interest, $S(Z)$ is the spillover term defined in Equation 2, $\rho$ is the spatial autoregressive coefficient governing dependence in the outcome beyond that induced by treatment and spillover, $X$ is the baseline incidence covariate with coefficient $\beta = 1$, and $\sigma = 1$. The spatial multiplier $(I-\rho W)^{-1}$ propagates each cluster's shocks through the network of neighbors. We tested $\rho \in \{0, 0.01, 0.20, 0.50\}$. When $\rho = 0$ the multiplier is the identity and the model is a linear regression with independent errors, $Y = \tau Z + S(Z) + \beta X + \epsilon$, in which spatial structure enters only through the spillover term; larger values of $\rho$ induce progressively stronger spatial clustering in the outcome.

We evaluated two spillover regimes,
$$
S(Z) = \gamma\, WZ \quad \text{(both arms)}, \qquad S(Z) = \gamma\, WZ \circ (1 - Z) \quad \text{(control only)}, \tag{2}
$$
where $\circ$ denotes the elementwise product. Under the control-only regime, only untreated clusters respond to the treatment status of their neighbors, which represents classical contamination: an untreated cluster's outcome rises with the share of its neighbors that are treated. Under the both-arms regime, every cluster responds to its neighbors' treatment regardless of its own assignment, so neighboring treatment adds to a treated cluster's own effect. We tested four spillover magnitudes, $\gamma \in \{0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8\}$, and five magnitudes of the direct effect, $\tau \in \{0.8, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0\}$, with $\tau = 1$ as the primary scenario throughout.

## Heterogeneous baseline incidence

Chapter 2 assumed a spatially uniform baseline outcome risk. Cluster-level health outcomes typically vary across space, and the designs studied here differ in whether and how they use that variation. We generated the baseline incidence covariate $X$, with values in $(0, 1)$, under three mechanisms. Under the independent (iid) mechanism, each $X_i$ is drawn from a Uniform$(0,1)$ distribution, with no spatial structure. Under the spatially autocorrelated mechanism, $X = \Phi\{(I - \rho_X W_Q)^{-1} u\}$, where $u \sim N(0, I)$, $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function applied elementwise, $W_Q$ is the queen weights matrix, and $\rho_X \in \{0.20, 0.50\}$. Under the Poisson mechanism, a spatially autocorrelated log-rate surface, $\log \lambda = \log(35/100{,}000) + (I - \rho_X W_Q)^{-1} u$ with $\rho_X \in \{0.20, 0.50\}$, generates cluster death counts $C_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i P)$, with an equal population of $P = 100{,}000$ in every cluster, so that a cluster at the base rate expects 35 deaths. The observed rates $C_i / P$ are then rank-normalized to $X_i = (r_i - 0.5)/N$, where $r_i$ is the rank of cluster $i$'s rate among the $N = 100$ clusters and tied rates share their average rank. Ties remain at this population size: the Poisson surfaces used here have between 60 and 76 distinct values among the 100 clusters. The base rate of 35 per 100,000 is taken from the sudden unexpected death (SUD) literature [@mirzaei_years_2019] to motivate the simulation. It is not the observed rate of the county data described in the Application section, which come from a different source, age range, period, and case definition. The incidence filters always use the queen weights $W_Q$, whichever neighbor type the scenario uses, so the incidence surfaces are identical under rook and queen contiguity. The iid mechanism and the two strengths of each of the other two mechanisms give five incidence configurations.

For each configuration we generated $K = 10$ incidence surfaces, $X_1, \dots, X_{10}$, each from its own seed. The same ten surfaces are used by every scenario in that configuration, across neighbor types, outcome-model parameters, designs, and values of $\tau$; only the design draws and the outcome noise differ across those scenarios. Each design is applied to the surface that generates the outcome: assignments for surface $k$ are drawn from $X_k$, and the outcome and the fitted model for those assignments use $X_k$ as well. This assumes that the incidence observed when a trial is planned is the incidence that drives its outcome. The target of each scenario is performance averaged over incidence surfaces; for example, $\text{MSE} = E_X E_{Z \mid X} E_\epsilon[(\hat\tau - \tau)^2]$, with $X$ drawn from the configuration's generator, $Z$ from the design given $X$, and $\epsilon \sim N(0, I)$. Bias, coverage, and power are defined in the same way.

## Treatment assignment designs

We implemented eight treatment assignment designs and present six of them as the primary comparison set in this chapter. The other two, Saturation Quadrants and Balanced Halves, each share the mechanism of a retained design, and in the eight-design comparison at $\tau = 1$ neither could be distinguished from its counterpart under either neighbor type. Saturation Quadrants assigns the saturations 20\%, 40\%, 60\%, and 80\% to the four quadrants in random order, without reference to incidence. Its mean squared error was 0.0900, against 0.0907 for Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants, under queen contiguity (Nemenyi $p = 0.98$; Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank $p = 0.41$), and 0.0708 against 0.0717 under rook contiguity (Nemenyi $p = 1.00$; Wilcoxon $p = 0.82$). We retain one representative of the saturation mechanism, Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants; that ordering the saturations by incidence makes no detectable difference is itself a result of this chapter. Balanced Halves divides clusters into two halves by incidence rank and treats 25 at random in each. Its mean squared error was 0.1299, against 0.1308 for Balanced Quartiles, under queen contiguity (Nemenyi $p = 1.00$; Wilcoxon $p = 0.88$), and 0.0842 against 0.0837 under rook contiguity (Nemenyi $p = 1.00$; Wilcoxon $p = 0.82$). The two designs differ only in how finely they stratify on incidence, and we retain the finer, four-stratum version; under queen contiguity Balanced Halves had the marginally lower mean, so this choice does not rest on performance. Both excluded designs, and the full eight-design comparison, are reported in the appendix of this chapter.

Table 1 describes the six retained designs. Checkerboard is the block-stratified design of Chapter 2, which called it Block Stratified Sampling; the two names refer to the same assignment, and we use Checkerboard in the rest of this chapter. Checkerboard is the only deterministic design: it gives the same assignment in every draw, although each of its fits still receives its own outcome noise. Every other design was drawn independently 25 times for each incidence surface. Designs that rank clusters by incidence break ties at random, afresh for each draw. High Incidence Focus is random only through that tie-breaking; under the iid and spatial mechanisms incidence values are distinct, so it gives the same assignment in all 25 draws on a surface, and its assignment changes only from one surface to the next. Isolation Buffer builds its assignment from the neighbor type of the scenario, and it treats 38 clusters on average under rook contiguity and 21 under queen contiguity. Every other design treats exactly 50.

## Estimation

We estimated $\tau$ with two maximum likelihood spatial lag models, both fit to every simulated outcome and both including an intercept. The primary, oracle model has the spatial lag $\rho WY$ and the covariates $Z$, $\text{Spill} = S(Z)$, and $X_k$, so it matches the outcome model in Equation 1, including the true regime-specific spillover covariate from Equation 2. The oracle model assumes that the analyst knows the form of the spillover mechanism and has the exact exposure term, so its results are a best case for each design; we return to this assumption as a limitation. The non-oracle model, a sensitivity analysis, has the covariates $Z$ and $X_k$ only and omits the spillover term. Both models are fit to the same outcomes.

We fit both models with our own implementation of the estimator computed by the `lagsarlm` function of the R package `spatialreg` with `method = "eigen"` [@bivand_comparing_2015]. It maximizes the concentrated log-likelihood over $\rho$, computing the log-determinant from the eigenvalues of $W$ [@ord_estimation_1975], estimates the remaining coefficients by least squares given $\hat\rho$, and computes standard errors from the analytic information matrix. On 5,120 validation fits it agreed with `lagsarlm` to within $9.7\times10^{-8}$ in $\hat\tau$ and to a relative difference of $1.1\times10^{-8}$ in its standard error, at roughly 1\% of the computing time; we also refit a 1\% sample of the full simulation with `lagsarlm` itself as a check. Confidence intervals are 95\% Wald intervals, $\hat\tau \pm 1.96\,\widehat{\text{SE}}$.

Two combinations of design and neighbor type weaken or remove the information that separates $\tau$ from the spillover term. Under rook contiguity, Checkerboard gives $WZ = 1 - Z$ exactly, because every neighbor of a treated cluster is a control and every neighbor of a control is treated. Both spillover covariates then equal $\gamma(1 - Z)$, a linear combination of the intercept and $Z$, so $\tau$ is not identified: the fitting routine drops the aliased spillover column, and the coefficient on $Z$ estimates $\tau - \gamma$. This is the "checkerboard paradox" of Chapter 2. The non-oracle model has no spillover column to drop, but its Checkerboard estimates under rook contiguity have the same defect. Under queen contiguity, each of the 64 interior clusters has four treated and four control neighbors, so $WZ = 1/2$ at every interior cluster, and only the 36 clusters on the grid boundary carry information that separates the spillover covariate from the intercept and $Z$; $\tau$ is identified, but imprecisely. Isolation Buffer under rook contiguity can also, rarely, draw exactly the checkerboard pattern, a maximal independent set that equals one color class of the grid. This happened in 4 of its 40,000 rook draws and affected one fit in each of 20 scenarios. We flag every fit in which the fitting routine reports an aliased column and every scenario in which some draw has $\text{rank}([1, Z, WZ]) < 3$. Aliased estimates are kept in all summaries and flagged in exhibits.

## Simulation design, resampling, and metrics

The full simulation crossed five values of $\tau$, five incidence configurations, two neighbor types, four values of $\rho$, four values of $\gamma$, two spillover regimes, and eight designs, for $5 \times 5 \times 2 \times 4 \times 4 \times 2 \times 8 = 12{,}800$ scenarios, of which the six designs reported in this chapter account for 9,600. We call a combination of incidence configuration, neighbor type, $\rho$, $\gamma$, and spillover regime a block; there are $5 \times 2 \times 4 \times 4 \times 2 = 320$ blocks, 160 for each neighbor type. At the primary scenario, $\tau = 1$, the six designs give 1,920 scenarios, and every block contains all six.

Within each scenario, we drew $J = 25$ assignments from each of the $K = 10$ incidence surfaces, for 250 fits per scenario, and gave every fit its own noise vector, so that fit $(k, j)$ has outcome $Y_{kj} = (I - \rho W)^{-1}[\tau Z_{kj} + S(Z_{kj}) + \beta X_k + \epsilon_{kj}]$. Checkerboard's 250 fits share one assignment but have 250 distinct noise vectors. Given a surface, its 25 pairs of assignment and noise are independent, and the ten surfaces are independent of one another, so the surface is the primary sampling unit. Each estimator was fit 3.2 million times.

Every random draw was seeded from a hash of a key that names the draw: the configuration and surface index for an incidence surface; the block, surface, and design for a set of 25 assignments; and the block for the noise. Each draw therefore depends only on its key, and the results are identical whether scenarios are run sequentially, in parallel, or in any order. The keys also give common random numbers. Within a block, all designs share the same noise vectors and incidence surfaces; the five values of $\tau$ reuse the same assignments and noise; and the oracle and non-oracle models are fit to the same outcomes. Assignments and noise are independent across blocks, but blocks within an incidence configuration share its ten surfaces.

For each scenario and estimator, we computed five metrics over the valid fits, those with a finite estimate and standard error: bias, the mean of $\hat\tau - \tau$; the standard deviation (SD) of $\hat\tau$; mean squared error, $\text{MSE} = \text{mean}\{(\hat\tau - \tau)^2\}$; coverage, the fraction of fits with $L \le \tau \le U$, where $L, U = \hat\tau \mp 1.96\,\widehat{\text{SE}}$; and power, the fraction of fits with $L > 0$, a one-sided test of $\tau = 0$ at level 0.025. For both estimators, every one of the 250 fits in every scenario was valid, and the fitting routine raised no warning other than the aliasing flags described above.

Monte Carlo standard errors come from the surface-level metrics. For a metric $m$, we computed $m_k$ on the 25 fits from surface $k$ and set $\text{SE}(m) = \text{sd}(m_1, \dots, m_{10})/\sqrt{10}$, with intervals $m \pm t_{0.975,\,9}\,\text{SE}(m)$. A difference between two designs is paired at the surface level: its standard error is that of $m_{d,k} - m_{d',k}$ over $k$.

We compared designs within each neighbor type with a Friedman rank-sum test on scenario MSE, treating the 160 blocks as repeated measures across the six designs. At $\tau = 1$ we followed it with Nemenyi post-hoc comparisons and Holm-adjusted paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for all 15 pairs of designs, and we repeated the Friedman test at each other value of $\tau$. Blocks within an incidence configuration share their surfaces, so these tests treat as independent blocks that are not, which overstates the information about variation from surface to surface. For each pair of designs adjacent in the ranking, we therefore also ran a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test over 50 independent units, the 5 configurations times 10 surfaces, with each unit's MSE averaged over that surface's blocks, and a $t_{49}$ interval for the mean difference. Because the values of $\tau$ share assignments and noise, Friedman tests at different values of $\tau$ are not independent confirmations of one another.

We report results separately for each neighbor type, with queen contiguity primary, and separately for each incidence configuration. Any number averaged over incidence configurations or over neighbor types is labeled as pooled, and we show the split wherever a conclusion changes.

# Results

## Design performance under queen contiguity

At the primary scenario, $\tau = 1$, under queen contiguity and pooled over the five incidence configurations, Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants had the lowest mean squared error (MSE = 0.091), followed by Balanced Quartiles (0.131), Isolation Buffer (0.160), High Incidence Focus (0.245), 2$\times$2 Blocking (0.319), and Checkerboard (1.087) (Table 2, Figure 1). Coverage of the 95\% intervals was between 0.936 and 0.941 for all six designs (Figure 2), so under queen contiguity the designs differed in precision, not in the validity of their intervals. Power to reject $\tau = 0$ was 0.930 for Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants, 0.827 for Balanced Quartiles, 0.731 for Isolation Buffer, 0.642 for 2$\times$2 Blocking, 0.610 for High Incidence Focus, and 0.547 for Checkerboard.

Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants also led block by block. Of the 160 queen blocks at $\tau = 1$, Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants had the lowest MSE in 95 (59\%), Balanced Quartiles in 58 (36\%), and Isolation Buffer in 7 (4\%); no other design had the lowest MSE in any block.

  MSE = c(0.079, 0.102, 0.133, 0.148, 0.228, 0.802),

## Formal statistical comparison

The Friedman test rejected equal MSE ranks across the six designs under queen contiguity at $\tau = 1$ ($\chi^2 = 451.57$, $\text{df} = 5$, 160 blocks, $p < 2.2\times10^{-16}$). The average within-block ranks were 1.43 for Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants, 2.14 for Balanced Quartiles, 3.69 for Isolation Buffer, 4.24 for 2$\times$2 Blocking, 4.74 for Checkerboard, and 4.76 for High Incidence Focus. Nemenyi comparisons (critical difference 0.596) separated 11 of the 15 pairs. Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants ranked significantly better than every other design, including Balanced Quartiles ($p = 0.0086$), and Balanced Quartiles ranked significantly better than the remaining four. The four pairs that Nemenyi comparisons did not separate all lay among the bottom four designs: 2$\times$2 Blocking against Isolation Buffer ($p = 0.090$), High Incidence Focus ($p = 0.130$), and Checkerboard ($p = 0.170$), and Checkerboard against High Incidence Focus ($p = 1.00$). Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank tests separated all 15 pairs.

The bottom three designs are ordered differently by average rank and by mean MSE. Checkerboard had the highest mean MSE but a slightly better average rank than High Incidence Focus, because its MSE depended strongly on the spillover regime: it had a low MSE under the both-arms regime (0.062, against 0.042 for the best design) and the highest MSE in every control-only block (see the spillover-regime results below). Mean MSE weights that control-only failure by its size; average rank counts it once per block.

Because blocks within an incidence configuration share their ten surfaces, we also compared each pair of designs adjacent in the mean-MSE order over the 50 independent configuration-by-surface units. Every adjacent pair differed significantly. The mean paired differences in MSE, with $t_{49}$ 95\% intervals, were $-0.0401$ ($-0.0431$, $-0.0372$) for Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants against Balanced Quartiles, $-0.0293$ ($-0.0332$, $-0.0255$) for Balanced Quartiles against Isolation Buffer, $-0.0853$ ($-0.0954$, $-0.0752$) for Isolation Buffer against High Incidence Focus, $-0.0738$ ($-0.0858$, $-0.0617$) for High Incidence Focus against 2$\times$2 Blocking, and $-0.7677$ ($-0.7893$, $-0.7460$) for 2$\times$2 Blocking against Checkerboard, with Wilcoxon $p \le 4.9\times10^{-9}$ in every case. The better design of each pair had the lower MSE in all 50 units, except High Incidence Focus against 2$\times$2 Blocking, where it did so in 48 (96\%). This test separated High Incidence Focus from 2$\times$2 Blocking, which the Nemenyi comparison did not, because it compares mean MSE rather than within-block ranks.

## Design rankings by incidence configuration

Within each of the five incidence configurations, the queen mean-MSE order was the same as the pooled order: Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants, Balanced Quartiles, Isolation Buffer, High Incidence Focus, 2$\times$2 Blocking, and Checkerboard. Across the five configurations, the MSE of Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants ranged from 0.087 (spatial, $\rho_X = 0.20$) to 0.093 (iid), that of Balanced Quartiles from 0.128 to 0.135, Isolation Buffer from 0.159 to 0.162, High Incidence Focus from 0.232 to 0.267, 2$\times$2 Blocking from 0.311 to 0.326, and Checkerboard from 1.068 to 1.112. Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants had the lowest MSE in 18 to 21 of the 32 blocks in each configuration. The mechanism that generated the incidence surface therefore changed each design's MSE only slightly and did not change the ranking. This includes High Incidence Focus, the design that uses the incidence ranks most directly: its MSE under the two Poisson configurations (0.232 and 0.238) was no higher than under the iid (0.245) and spatial (0.267 and 0.245) configurations.

## Sensitivity to spatial dependence, spillover magnitude, and spillover regime

Under queen contiguity, neither the strength of spatial dependence in the outcome nor the spillover magnitude changed the ranking. Across $\rho \in \{0, 0.01, 0.20, 0.50\}$, no design's MSE changed by more than 0.02 (Table 3). Across $\gamma \in \{0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8\}$, the MSE of every design except Checkerboard also varied by less than 0.02, and Checkerboard's varied between 1.052 and 1.108 with no trend in $\gamma$ (Table 4). Under rook contiguity, $\gamma$ mattered for Checkerboard alone, for the reason given in the rook results below.

The spillover regime was the one factor that changed the queen ranking (Table 5, Figure 1). Under the both-arms regime, Balanced Quartiles had the lowest MSE (0.042), followed by Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants (0.046), 2$\times$2 Blocking (0.062), Checkerboard (0.062), Isolation Buffer (0.161), and High Incidence Focus (0.162). Under the control-only regime, the order was Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants (0.135), Isolation Buffer (0.159), Balanced Quartiles (0.219), High Incidence Focus (0.329), 2$\times$2 Blocking (0.576), and Checkerboard (2.111). Isolation Buffer's MSE was the same under both regimes (0.161 and 0.159) by construction: no treated cluster has a treated neighbor, so $WZ = 0$ at every treated cluster, $WZ \circ (1 - Z) = WZ$, and the two regimes in Equation 2 define the same outcome model; the small difference is Monte Carlo error, since the two regimes use separate draws. Every other design had a higher MSE under the control-only regime.

That increase was variance, not bias. The oracle model contains the exact regime-specific spillover covariate, so omitting a spillover term cannot bias it. In every combination of design and regime under queen contiguity, the absolute bias was at most 0.048 and squared bias was less than 2\% of MSE. Checkerboard shows the mechanism most clearly. At its 64 interior clusters, $WZ = 1/2$. Under the both-arms regime the spillover covariate is therefore the constant $\gamma/2$ at those clusters, confounded with the intercept but not with $Z$. Under the control-only regime it equals $(\gamma/2)(1 - Z)$ there, a linear combination of the intercept and $Z$, so only the 36 boundary clusters separate the spillover effect from the treatment effect. Checkerboard's MSE rose from 0.062 under the both-arms regime to 2.111 under the control-only regime, while its bias stayed near zero (0.004) and its coverage stayed at 0.942: its intervals widened with its variance. Its pooled MSE of 1.087 was almost entirely variance, with mean squared bias below $10^{-5}$ (Figure 3 shows the decomposition for the Poisson configuration with $\rho_X = 0.20$). 2$\times$2 Blocking showed the same pattern on a smaller scale, with MSE rising from 0.062 to 0.576 and a bias of 0.016 under the control-only regime.

Two designs were therefore fragile with respect to the spillover regime, which a trial team cannot know in advance. Under queen contiguity, Checkerboard and 2$\times$2 Blocking were close to the best designs under the both-arms regime and were the two worst under the control-only regime. Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants was first or second under both regimes.

## Rook contiguity

Under rook contiguity at $\tau = 1$, pooled over the five incidence configurations, the mean-MSE order was Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants (0.072), Balanced Quartiles (0.084), 2$\times$2 Blocking (0.128), Isolation Buffer (0.133), High Incidence Focus (0.206), and Checkerboard (0.480) (Table 2), and the same order held within each of the five incidence configurations. Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants had the lowest MSE in 97 of the 160 rook blocks (61\%) and Balanced Quartiles in 60 (38\%). Coverage was between 0.938 and 0.942 for every design except Checkerboard, whose coverage was 0.150. The Friedman test rejected equal ranks ($\chi^2 = 703.76$, $\text{df} = 5$, 160 blocks, $p < 2.2\times10^{-16}$). Nemenyi comparisons separated 13 of 15 pairs; the two they did not separate were Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants against Balanced Quartiles ($p = 0.74$) and 2$\times$2 Blocking against Isolation Buffer ($p = 1.00$). Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon tests separated every pair except 2$\times$2 Blocking against Isolation Buffer. In the surface-level comparison, Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants had a lower MSE than Balanced Quartiles in 48 of the 50 units (mean difference $-0.0121$; $-0.0139$, $-0.0102$; Wilcoxon $p = 9.9\times10^{-10}$). 2$\times$2 Blocking and Isolation Buffer were close: 2$\times$2 Blocking had the lower MSE in 36 of the 50 units (72\%; mean difference $-0.0048$; $-0.0078$, $-0.0017$; Wilcoxon $p = 0.0027$), but Isolation Buffer had the slightly better average rank (3.38 against 3.40), and the two designs traded places at some values of $\tau$ (see the results for $\tau$ below). Every other adjacent pair differed in all 50 units.

Checkerboard under rook contiguity is a different case: $\tau$ is not identified. Because $WZ = 1 - Z$ exactly, both spillover covariates equal $\gamma(1 - Z)$, and the coefficient on $Z$ estimates $\tau - \gamma$. The estimates behaved accordingly. At $\tau = 1$, Checkerboard's mean bias was $-0.502$, $-0.600$, $-0.704$, and $-0.802$ at $\gamma = 0.5$, 0.6, 0.7, and 0.8, while its standard deviation stayed between 0.20 and 0.21; mean squared bias accounted for 0.425 of its MSE of 0.480. Its coverage fell from 0.316 at $\gamma = 0.5$ to 0.027 at $\gamma = 0.8$. Its MSE was the same under both regimes (0.477 and 0.483), as expected when the two spillover covariates coincide. Under queen contiguity, by contrast, Checkerboard's coverage stayed between 0.939 and 0.943 at every level of $\rho$; under rook contiguity it was between 0.134 and 0.161 (Table 6). Rook Checkerboard estimates were precise but centered on the wrong quantity, the opposite of its imprecise but valid queen estimates. This is the checkerboard paradox of Chapter 2, reproduced on a grid of 100 clusters; we return to the connection with Chapter 2 in the Discussion. We keep these estimates in every ranking and flag them.

## Non-oracle sensitivity analysis

The non-oracle model, which omits the spillover term, was biased for every design. At $\tau = 1$, and setting aside Checkerboard under rook contiguity, its bias ranged from $-0.12$ to $-0.40$ and its coverage from 0.51 to 0.90 across designs and neighbor types. Under queen contiguity its bias ranged from $-0.123$ (Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants) to $-0.244$ (2$\times$2 Blocking) and its coverage from 0.709 (2$\times$2 Blocking) to 0.896 (High Incidence Focus); under rook contiguity the most biased design was Isolation Buffer (bias $-0.400$, coverage 0.513). For Checkerboard under rook contiguity, the non-oracle estimates were identical to the oracle estimates (MSE 0.480, bias $-0.652$, coverage 0.150), because once the aliased spillover column is dropped the two models are the same.

Omitting the spillover term also removes a column that can be nearly collinear with $Z$, and the non-oracle estimates were accordingly less variable for some designs. Under queen contiguity, the non-oracle MSE was lower than the oracle MSE for every design, most of all for Checkerboard (oracle 1.087, non-oracle 0.108) and 2$\times$2 Blocking (oracle 0.319, non-oracle 0.121). Under rook contiguity it was higher for every design except 2$\times$2 Blocking (0.128 under both models) and Checkerboard (identical). These results do not change the recommendation. Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants also had the lowest non-oracle MSE under both neighbor types (0.087 under queen contiguity and 0.086 under rook contiguity), and where a design's non-oracle MSE was lower, the estimate was biased and its intervals under-covered, so the lower MSE does not support valid inference.

## Stability across treatment effect sizes

Under queen contiguity, the design order was the same at every $\tau \in \{0.8, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0\}$, whether designs were ordered by average within-block rank or by mean MSE (Figure 4). The Friedman statistic was 455.49, 451.57, 429.01, 411.19, and 376.79 at these five values ($p < 2.2\times10^{-16}$ at each). The margin between the two leading designs narrowed as $\tau$ increased: the average rank of Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants rose from 1.41 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 1.85 at $\tau = 3$, while that of Balanced Quartiles stayed between 2.13 and 2.14, and the MSE of Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants rose from 0.088 to 0.115 while that of Isolation Buffer stayed at 0.160. Under rook contiguity the order was also stable except for the close pair of 2$\times$2 Blocking and Isolation Buffer: by average rank, 2$\times$2 Blocking was ahead only at $\tau = 0.8$, and by mean MSE, Isolation Buffer was ahead only at $\tau = 3$. The five values of $\tau$ share their assignments and noise, so these five comparisons are not independent confirmations of one another; they show that the order does not depend on the size of the effect, given the same draws.

## Robustness across blocks and the recommended design

Table 7 gives the distribution of MSE across the 160 queen blocks at $\tau = 1$. Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants had the lowest median (0.080) and the lowest worst-case MSE of any design (0.169). Isolation Buffer had the narrowest range (0.128 to 0.206), because its MSE does not depend on the spillover regime, but at a higher level. Balanced Quartiles had a low median (0.115) and a worst case of 0.290. The distributions of 2$\times$2 Blocking and Checkerboard reflect their dependence on the spillover regime: both had low first quartiles (0.062 and 0.063) and high upper quartiles (0.580 and 2.093). Checkerboard had the highest MSE in all 80 control-only blocks; in the 80 both-arms blocks, the highest MSE belonged to High Incidence Focus in 42 and to Isolation Buffer in 38. Under rook contiguity, Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants also had the lowest worst-case MSE (0.138).

We recommend Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants. It had the lowest mean MSE under both neighbor types, in every incidence configuration, at every value of $\tau$, and under the control-only regime; its worst case across blocks was the lowest of the six designs; and its intervals had coverage of 0.937 under queen contiguity and 0.942 under rook contiguity. Balanced Quartiles also performed well. It was second overall under both neighbor types and was marginally better than Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants only under the both-arms regime (0.0421 against 0.0459 under queen contiguity, 0.0421 against 0.0451 under rook contiguity), where Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants had the lower MSE in 22 of 80 queen blocks and 23 of 80 rook blocks. Under the control-only regime, Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants had the lower MSE in all 80 queen blocks and 75 of 80 rook blocks, by a wider margin (0.135 against 0.219 under queen contiguity).

The performance of Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants does not come from ordering the saturations by incidence. Saturation Quadrants, which assigns the same four saturations to the quadrants in random order, had an MSE of 0.0900 against 0.0907 under queen contiguity and 0.0708 against 0.0717 under rook contiguity, and the two designs could not be distinguished (see Methods). What the two designs share, treating the four quadrants at fixed saturations of 20\% to 80\%, is what separated them from the other designs. Coverage did not separate the designs: it was close to 0.94 for every design under both neighbor types, except Checkerboard under rook contiguity, where $\tau$ is not identified.

# Application: A Planned Sudden Unexpected Death Prevention Pilot in North Carolina

## Background

Sudden unexpected death (SUD) in adults is a substantial and incompletely understood cause of premature mortality. The SUDDEN (Sudden Unexpected Death in North Carolina) methodology, a validated algorithm for classifying deaths as sudden and unexpected from death certificate and medical record data, was developed and screened against expert physician panel review by Nanavati and colleagues [@nanavati_sudden_2014]. Using this methodology, Mirzaei and colleagues estimated a North Carolina SUD base rate of approximately 35 per 100,000 among adults aged 20--64 and found that the resulting years of life lost and productivity loss from SUD exceed that of any individual cancer, underscoring SUD's substantial and under-recognized public health burden [@mirzaei_years_2019]. Subsequent work has documented substantial geographic and socioeconomic gradients in SUD incidence within North Carolina specifically: Gan and colleagues found elevated SUD incidence in rural counties relative to urban counties [@gan_factors_2019], and Mounsey and colleagues found an inverse relationship between household income and SUD incidence in Wake County [@mounsey_relation_2017]. Together, this literature establishes both that SUD is a meaningful and measurable outcome in North Carolina and that its incidence varies spatially and socioeconomically in ways that are directly relevant to the incidence-informed designs evaluated in this chapter.

## The planned pilot design

A pilot intervention is being planned in collaboration with North Carolina's community college (CC) system, which offers a natural spatial and organizational unit for the design framework developed in this chapter. North Carolina's 58 community colleges collectively serve all 100 counties in the state; each college has a primary campus in one county and, in many cases, satellite campuses in neighboring counties (for example, Durham Technical Community College operates a satellite campus in Orange County in addition to its primary Durham County campus). This network structure is a direct, real-world analog of the spillover mechanism modeled throughout this chapter, because community colleges within a shared service network communicate and coordinate programmatic activity with one another; an intervention delivered at one college plausibly influences outcomes at a neighboring college's service area even without any formal expansion of the intervention itself, exactly as the spillover term $\gamma WZ$ in Equation 1 models diffusion between spatially adjacent clusters.

The planned pilot site is Lenoir Community College, whose service area comprises Lenoir, Greene, and Jones counties; the pilot cluster is that whole service area, with anticipated spillover to adjacent CC service areas; the pilot intervention involves workforce development and disaster-response-style training intended to empower CC students and staff to recognize signs of medical distress, connect at-risk individuals to care, and support timely follow-up. Because the teaching intervention under consideration is delivered county-wide by design, rather than at finer spatial resolution such as the census tract level, the natural treatment unit for this application is the CC service area (equivalently, a group of one or more counties) rather than the census tract, notwithstanding that individual-level incidence data may still be collected at finer resolution to inform the incidence-aware design components. The eventual evaluation plan anticipates that the intervention's effect will be visible first in intermediate process measures, such as medication adherence and the timeliness of clinic visits following an at-risk event, since meaningful shifts in the SUD incidence rate itself are not expected to be detectable on the timescale of an initial pilot; this expected measurement lag between process outcomes and the ultimate incidence outcome modeled throughout this chapter is discussed further as a limitation below.

County-level SUD incidence for 2018--2021 was derived by Habib from North Carolina death certificates [@habib_temporal_2026]. Of the 412,514 deaths recorded statewide over that period, that derivation kept the 111,665 deaths among working-age adults (aged 18--64). It excluded deaths in hospitals and other institutions and deaths from expected causes (such as trauma, overdose, COVID-19, and end-stage chronic disease), and it applied a death-certificate algorithm validated against the SUDDEN physician-adjudicated cohort [@gan_factors_2019; @nanavati_sudden_2014]. The result is 21,147 sudden unexpected out-of-hospital deaths among working-age adults, pooled to the county level using death-certificate zip codes, with population-at-risk denominators from Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) data for the corresponding years. We then aggregate these county-level data to the 58 community college service-area clusters. These data are not yet available for use in this dissertation chapter: access to them requires joining an active institutional review board protocol governing the SUDDEN dataset, a process that is underway at the time of this writing. Planned covariates for the eventual real-data application, once finalized, include county-level median income, food-desert status, physician access, and average driving distance to the nearest hospital, none of which are incorporated into the placeholder illustration below.

## A preliminary, explicitly placeholder illustration

As a preliminary illustration only, and not as a finalized design recommendation, we re-ran the six-design comparison pipeline over the actual 58-cluster CC service-area geography, using dissolved county-level service boundaries and Queen contiguity, rather than the abstract $10\times10$ regular grid used in the primary comparison above. Because real SUD incidence data is not yet available, the baseline incidence surface used in this application run is a synthetic placeholder, generated from a Poisson spatial autoregressive process calibrated to the same 35-per-100,000 base rate reported above, with population drawn from 2024 North Carolina Office of State Budget and Management county population estimates. \textbf{The numeric results reported in this subsection are a simulated placeholder and must not be interpreted as a design recommendation for the real application}; they will be superseded once the real SUDDEN-derived county dataset described above is finalized and substituted for the synthetic incidence surface.

With that caveat stated clearly, the qualitative pattern observed on this real, irregular geography was consistent with the primary grid-based comparison reported above: designs that stratify or saturate treatment according to incidence (Balanced Quartiles and the saturation-family designs) again achieved the lowest average MSE, in the range of 0.075--0.078, while a design adapted from the grid-based Checkerboard concept and a design that ignores incidence entirely (High Incidence Focus, applied without a reliable real incidence signal) performed markedly worse, with average MSE above 0.23. This qualitative consistency across a substantially different, irregular real-world geography is reassuring evidence that the primary comparison's conclusions are not an artifact specific to the regular $10\times10$ grid, though it is not a substitute for repeating the full comparison once real incidence data replace the synthetic placeholder.

# Discussion

## Summary and relevance

This chapter provides, to our knowledge, the first systematic, simulation-based comparison of multiple conceptually distinct treatment assignment strategies for spatial cluster randomized trials under heterogeneous, rather than uniform, baseline outcome incidence. Its central finding is that treatment assignment design, chosen before a trial begins, can materially reduce estimation error and preserve valid statistical inference under spatial spillover, without requiring any change to the analysis-stage estimator. It suggests that a trial team choosing among a small number of concrete assignment strategies, at the pre-registration stage of a spatial CRT, can substantially improve their study's expected performance by preferring incidence-informed saturation or stratification designs and by explicitly avoiding a design intuition imported from non-spatial CRT practice, namely that maximizing physical separation between treatment arms is a conservative, safe default. In this simulation, that intuition failed: Checkerboard's maximal spatial separation between treated and control clusters was the single worst-performing strategy on both estimation accuracy and inferential validity, and its failure was shown, through the parameter sensitivity analysis above, to be specifically and monotonically driven by the magnitude of the spillover coefficient rather than by outcome spatial dependence more broadly. This is a design-stage complement to the existing analysis-stage literature reviewed in the Introduction, not a substitute for it; a well-chosen design reduces the burden placed on post-hoc statistical correction, but does not eliminate the value of spatial regression modeling, which was used as the estimator for every design compared in this chapter.

## Limitations

Several limitations bound the conclusions drawn here and motivate the future work outlined below. First, and most significantly, we used an oracle maximum likelihood specification throughout, in which the true spillover exposure term was supplied to the estimator as a known covariate. This represents a best-case bound on estimation performance under each design; a non-oracle specification, in which an analyst must estimate or approximate the spillover structure without knowing it in advance, would be expected to show more uniformly degraded performance across all designs, and the relative ranking among designs under a realistic, non-oracle estimation strategy remains an open empirical question. Second, the outcome model held the incidence coefficient $\beta$ fixed at 1 throughout and assumed equal population size across all clusters in the Poisson incidence mode; the real North Carolina application described above, by contrast, involves substantially heterogeneous county and CC-service-area populations, and heterogeneous population sizes may alter the relative performance of incidence-informed designs in ways not captured by the equal-population simulation reported here. Third, the primary comparison used a regular $10\times10$ lattice with queen contiguity, a geometry chosen for computational tractability and ease of interpretation rather than realism; the preliminary application-scale illustration on the actual 58-cluster CC network geography, reported above, suggests the qualitative design ranking is at least broadly robust to this simplification, but the grid size and regularity were not themselves systematically varied as an experimental factor. Fourth, and specific to the applied setting, the process-versus-incidence outcome measurement lag noted above, in which meaningful SUD rate changes are not expected to be detectable on the timescale of an initial pilot, means that the eventual real-data evaluation of the design framework developed in this chapter will need to rely on intermediate process outcomes (medication adherence, timely clinic visits) as a proxy for the incidence-based outcome modeled throughout the simulation study, and the relationship between design performance on an incidence outcome and design performance on a process-outcome proxy has not been separately established.

## Future work

Several extensions follow directly from the limitations above and are natural next steps for this line of work. Relaxing the oracle estimation assumption, by evaluating design performance under a non-oracle spatial regression specification that does not assume the analyst knows the true spillover exposure term, is the highest-priority extension, since it would test whether the design-stage advantages documented here survive under estimation conditions a real analyst would actually face. Incorporating heterogeneous cluster population sizes into the Poisson incidence-generating mechanism would bring the simulation closer to the real North Carolina application, where county and CC-service-area populations vary substantially. Evaluating design performance directly and systematically on irregular, real-world geographies at multiple scales, rather than treating the CC-network application as a single confirmatory check, would clarify how much of the grid-based ranking generalizes broadly versus reflecting properties specific to a regular lattice. Finally, and most immediately, applying the design-selection framework developed in this chapter to the real SUDDEN-derived North Carolina county dataset, once data access and IRB processes described above are finalized, is the next step of this work and will determine whether the design recommendations illustrated here as a simulated placeholder hold under real, observed incidence heterogeneity.
